cells.tense: you're standing at the door as things arrive, and your hands are open, not clenched — nothing's being rushed and nothing's being held down.
cells.ask: offer what's just landed enough room to take its own shape, and see what grows when you're not the one growing it.
cells.core: You're at the door as things come in, and your hands are open instead of clenched. Whatever's arriving gets tended without being hurried and without being pinned — you give it what it needs and then let it get on with the growing. Nothing here is being forced, and nothing is being clutched.\n\nThat kind of patience isn't passivity. It's what makes the care you give able to feed the next thing without draining you, because you're not gripping the outcome. Give this arriving thing more room than it seems to need. The tending still works when you're not the one standing over it watching, and that ease stays in your hands.
cells.sheetLine: Things arrive, you tend them without a grip, and they grow.
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside arrives and asks to be met

cells.tense: you're leaning past the door into a future you can't write yet, and your hands are already on whatever's arriving before it has a chance to land.
cells.ask: let one thing that's arriving stay unknown a little longer — meet the next step without mapping the whole road.
cells.core: You're already shaping what's arriving before it's fully here — reaching forward, adjusting, making sure it turns out right. The reaching is care, and it's also ahead of itself. What's off is the timing: you're tending a future that hasn't been handed to you, which means the present thing never gets met on its own terms.\n\nIn its good form, the arriving thing gets carried the way you'd carry something you trust to grow — close attention, no grip. You can get back to that by letting one thing stay unknown a little longer. Take the next step with only enough light for that step, and a door opens because you didn't force it — and the opening gives you back the next step.
cells.sheetLine: You're controlling what's arriving before it's yours.
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside arrives and asks to be met

cells.tense: you're standing back from the door that's already behind you, not reaching for what's arriving now, calling the distance independence.
cells.ask: name one thing you'd genuinely want to grow, and take one small step toward tending it this week.
cells.core: You're not at the door. You stepped back sometime ago and called the distance independence — but nothing's being invited in and nothing's being tended. What's arriving now goes unmet, and the not-met is starting to feel like there's nothing worth meeting.\n\nIn its good form, the door is a lively place: things come in, you reach for them, and the reaching feeds you. The way back starts with wanting something. Name one thing you'd genuinely want to grow — not the thing you were handed to want — and take one small step toward it. Desire pulls the reach back into your hands, and the reach is what makes arriving possible again, one small wanting at a time.
cells.sheetLine: You've stepped back from the door and called it independence.
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside arrives and asks to be met

cells.tense: you're already at the door doing the caring, and it's running while you talk about it as if it were just how things are.
cells.ask: let one piece of the tending that's been running on its own go — and keep the one you'd actually choose.
cells.core: You're the one at the door, taking in what's arriving, tending it — and you'd tell it as just the way things are. The work is real. You're just not counted as the one doing it, and that's why the whole thing feels like weight instead of choice.\n\nIn its good form, the tending is yours and you know it — you pick what to carry and what to set down. So let one piece go, the one that's been running by itself. Keeping the piece you actually choose is what turns depletion back into a door you're standing at on purpose, and the choosing is what makes it yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're the caretaker here and you call it just how it is.
